Polar bear attacks documentary film team - International buy in [6017]

By: SimonStanford | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Polar bear attacks documentary film team in north east Greenland.

Unique Selling Point:
South African documentary film maker, Simon Stanford was on assignment in remote north east Greenland when he and his team were attacked by a hungry polar bear.

Summary:
South African documentary film maker, Simon Stanford together with award winning underwater cameraman, Göran Ehlmé and biologist Lars Knutsen set off for Young Sound in remote north east Greenland to make a film about walrus. The plan was to follow Göran who had won the prestigious world wildlife photographer of the year award for his pictures of walrus foraging on the bottom of the sound while he dived again with new high resolution cameras. The film, How To Meet A Walrus, aims to highlight the difficulties faced by natural history film makers in this challenging arctic environment but the main focus is on the walrus and how they are being forced to adapt to the rapid changes that climate instability has wrought on their environment. After just 2 weeks they were caught up in a dramatic turn of events when a hungry polar bear forced open a window in their cabin and tried to drag, biologist, Lars Knutsen out and eat him. Polar bears are rarely seen on this stretch of coast during the short arctic summer but this year the sea ice retreated so fast and so far that a large number were stranded on the mainland, separated from the seals that are their normal prey. Consequently a group of increasingly hungry bears started to look at walrus and humans as prey.

Script:


Polar bears Greenland 6017


Names:

Göran Ehlmé: Underwater Photographer
Lars Øivind Knutsen: Biologist




Tc: 00:03 Location/ Date text: Stockholm Sweden 12 July 2021 58.40 N 16.16 E,

Simon Stanford on camera while packing:

I’m busy packing all the camera equipment for a trip to Greenland next week. I’m going together with 2 other people to film for a documentary that has the working title, How To Meet A Walrus.

Simon VO:

To meet a walrus in it’s arctic environment the man to call is award winning underwater photographer, Göran Ehlmé and to help me to understand them, who better than Lars Öivind Knutsen, film maker and biologist who has spent many years studying these giant marine mammals. Lars and Göran have visited Young Sound and filmed the walrus on several occasions over the years and Göran’s photographs of walrus feeding on the sea bed won him the prestigious world wildlife photographer of the year award.

Göran Ehlmé:

It was super exciting. When we took off from Konstabel Point it was really rough weather
but as we flew further north it’s.. as you can see, fantastic weather.
We flew in over Sandö and there lay 10 to 15 walrus
on the beach just waiting for us.
We’re really excited now.

Simon VO:

Location graphic: Daneborg research Station NE Greenland 17 July 2021 -74.30 N, -20.23 E
Our base for the next month is Daneborg research station which is run by the “Greenland Ecosystem Monitoring Programme”. Not far off is a small Danish military outpost.

We will use the coming weeks to film walrus underwater, a challenge that was considered too dangerous until Göran filmed his award winning material in 2005. While Göran concentrates on filming underwater I will document as much as I can of the fjord and its surrounds. My objective is to document the walrus and to get an insight into what environmental changes they are experiencing and how they are adapting.
But our assignment will soon take a dangerous and extreme twist we will face a challenge from an unexpected quarter a challenge we will come to understand to be fuelled by climate change.

Lars Öivind Knutsen:

They don’t seem particularly worried about my presence.
They’re rather slow on land so there is no real threat here for me.
They don’t stand a chance of catching up to me here.
On the other hand if you meet a big walrus in the water
It’s a totally different story.
There, they are like a cheetah, incredibly graceful and fast under water.





Göran Ehlmé:

It was not until the 3rd year or the third time I was here that I dared to make an attempt to get close. And obviously during that first encounter I was extremely nervous.
The problem is that the walrus is eating in relatively shallow water which means that he is making the water very cloudy from 3 meters down to the bottom which makes it difficult for me to know in which cloud of sediment the walrus is hidden.
I found a walrus on one attempt. I was just behind him and saw his back flippers and managed to come up alongside him. The problem then is that he sees me because I have come so close and he gets a bit nervous.


Simon VO:
Every day is a new challenge we are now diving up to 15 times a day but we are getting closer to achieving that magic moment. Diving in this arctic fjord is spectacular. Icebergs create their only magical ecosystem and there is plenty for us to film.

But all is not as it should be!
The walrus have become skittish, the normally cold arctic weather is interspersed with days that reach record high temperatures of over 20°c and the snow and ice becomes more and more scarce.

When we landed on Greenland we were instructed on how to behave in the unlikely event that we should encounter polar bear. For me this is an exciting possibility but I’m not holding my breath so when we get a radio call from the military base to say that a polar bear has been sighted near to the base.

TC 4:30 Location graphic: Daneborg Military Base NE Greenland 2 August 2021, 74.30N, 20.23E

Göran and I race back to try and get what we consider to be a rare opportunity to film one of these magnificent creatures.
We spent an hour or two searching and eventually give up and go back to base.

Simon On Camera:

What you see in the foreground of this picture are fresh polar bear tracks. We are here to do a film about walrus but we’ve been completely distracted by the huge number of polar bear that have actually chased off the walrus from this island where they would normally rest.

Simon VO

And rest was what I have in mind while I make coffee back at basecamp. While in the kitchen I sense movement outside the window, look up and there it is not more that 15 meters away. I see my first polar bear. He is exactly as I expected, magnificent. It is immediately very clear that this is his territory and that we are the intruders. We keep our distance but still get some great pictures and go to bed this night satisfied that we have managed to film another iconic arctic species and confident that we will soon be back on track with the walrus but the polar bear has other ideas.

Simon VO:

It’s just after 5 o’clock on Monday morning the 2nd of august. We’ve been here on Greenland for nearly 3 weeks now. If you look behind me here this mosquito net is torn wide open and there is a mess here and bear paw prints all over the window.

LÖ:
We are staying in what is in principle a normal house. I left my window open a crack.

Göran:
At 4 am on Monday morning I was woken to hear Lars Öivind.


Simon:

The most terrifying scream.

LÖ:
The bear had lifted the window and stood with both his front paws and his head in my room.

Simon:
It grabbed him by his left hand pulled him over and was trying to pull him out the window.

LÖ:
It pulled and pulled and pulled. I screamed and screamed and screamed. Total panic I stood face to face with a bear and he was trying to pull me out the window by my arm. I tried to pull back, screamed and tried to hit him with my other hand and it refused to let go.

Simon:
I then heard Göran beginning to shout as well and I though, oh my god, hes gone out to rescue Lars Öivind and he’s been attacked.

Göran:
I grabbed the broom that was standing by the door and threw it at the bear, hit it on its side, it backed off a meter or so.

Simon:
So I ran out the door grabbing the signal pistol on the way and the bear Wass not more than 2,5 metres away just outside LÖ’s window. It had actually just let him go so I fired the signal pistol over its head head it makes a very big loud flash and a bang and the bear backed off and we stood looking at each other for maybe 2 seconds and I realised that it was going to need a little bit more so I fired a 2nd shot and….



Göran:
So that scared the bear so he ran off down the beach. So we got the situation under control, more or less.


Simon:
We were pretty shocked but we managed to patch LÖ up. He was bleeding very heavily. We couldn’t see the extent of the wound because it was so bloody. There were a lot of scratches because the bear had tried to pull him close with its claws.

LÖ Knutsen:
I've obviously always had respect for bears but maybe after working with them for so long one can have become a bit too familiar and begin to think this will go fine, its always been fine but I now feel shocked of course but also afraid, I don’t want to go and sleep in that same room again tonight. We’ll see how we do.

TC 8:03: Location Date Graphic: Berghaus Point NE Greenland 4 August 2021, 74.2N, -20.09E

Bear running along beach

Simon on Camera:
So about 5 minutes ago a young bear passed here. These are his tracks along the beach. This is definitely the same bear that nearly put us at the wrong end of the food chain last night.

Normally there would be pack ice further north from here where the bears can hunt seals as is their custom. We can only speculate now why there is such big accumulation of polar bears in this area where we are based.

LÖ Knutsen:
The Greenland sea lies before us and it is totally ice free. There is no pack ice out there as would be normal at this time of year. There isn’t even any pack ice further north where there would normally be plenty and that’s where the polar bears would normally be at this season. They are totally dependent on seals to survive the summers. Seals particularly a species called ringed seals would normally rest one the ice when they are not hunting and that is where the polar bears would normally in their turn must them. So the ice is in fact crucial to the survival of polar bears through the whole year.

Simon VO:

The time we spent on Greenland was dramatic. The walrus have come and gone. Our encounter with polar bear went from fascinating to traumatic. The weather swung from one extreme to the next. We never did get the images of walrus feeding on the sea bottom that we were aiming for but we experienced so much more. A short summer is not enough to be able to draw conclusions about what we saw other than that we witnessed an environment that is undergoing rapid and dramatic changes that profoundly effect the animals we came here to film.
